Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
ruminate about how event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma defined as witnessing domestic violence, 'Body Shame' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type because it implies a direct bodily violation or injury to the patient rather than witnessing violence between others. While witness trauma can lead to guilt, fear, mistrust, or betrayal appraisals, shame specifically about 'what happened to my body' is clinically implausible here unless there is an additional unreported direct trauma.

issues.item: Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
issues.explanation: The memory profile centers on disorganized, overwhelmed recall of a witnessed domestic violence event. 'Auditory Recall' can occur in witness trauma, but in this profile it is the only strongly sensory-perceptual memory item and is not linked to any trigger items or matching contextual content. Given the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from Memory and the rest of the profile emphasizes global threat and appraisal-driven coping, this item stands out as poorly integrated and may reflect a different trauma presentation.

vignette: Sofia, a 26-year-old Latina school counselor, has been haunted by memories of domestic violence she witnessed in childhood. Growing up, her home was not the sanctuary it should have been. Instead, it was a place where tension and fear were palpable. The violent episodes between her parents left lasting scars on her psyche, manifesting as a pervasive sense of threat and an inability to trust others. Sofia's perception that the institutions meant to protect her had let her down fostered deep mistrust towards people. She believed that if only someone had intervened, she would not be experiencing these overwhelming emotions today. This institutional failure compounded with self-blame led her to feel responsible for the events, a belief that further fueled her hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors. At work, Sofia's heightened vigilance made it difficult to connect authentically with students. She felt an intense need to monitor everyone around her, always on guard against potential threats. This hyperalertness extended into her home life; she couldn't relax even within the four walls of her own apartment, needing to keep her back pressed against a wall where she could see everything in the room. The slightest unexpected touch would cause her to startle, as if reverting to that childhood state of constant fear. These behaviors were not just reactions but deeply ingrained strategies shaped by her traumatic experiences. Memories of her parents' arguments and violence would often return without warning, triggered by mundane sights or sounds. When these memories surfaced, Sofia was overwhelmed with emotions, making it hard for her to function. She struggled to explain what she had witnessed clearly, losing the thread of her narrative mid-conversation. The memory intrusions exacerbated her hypervigilance and mistrust. Every time a memory flooded back-triggered perhaps by the sound of raised voices or an argumentative tone in a colleague's voice-Sofia would retreat into herself, ruminating on how she could have prevented the violence. This rumination reinforced her belief that people were not to be trusted, and institutions had failed her. Her fear of being hurt again made going back to places reminiscent of those traumatic events nearly impossible. The school where she worked often became a trigger when students acted out in ways that reminded her of her own childhood experiences. These moments would set off a cycle of hypervigilance, making it difficult for her to focus and connect with her students. Sofia's sense of threat was not just confined to her work environment but permeated her daily life. The more she felt unsafe, the more she ruminated on how things could have been prevented, deepening her self-blame. This cycle tightened around her, making it increasingly difficult for her to feel secure or trust others. Her hypervigilance extended beyond just keeping her back against a wall; she avoided social gatherings and even close friendships because of her fear of being touched unexpectedly or feeling unsafe in unfamiliar settings. These avoidance behaviors led to isolation, further intensifying her negative appraisals about people and institutions. Sofia finally sought help when her work performance began to suffer severely, marked by frequent absences and an inability to provide the emotional support needed for her students. She was most afraid of being overwhelmed again but also hopeful that therapy could help her process these memories and regain a sense of safety in her daily life.
